content:
I fully admit that my DIY-modified iPhone camera looks pretty ridiculous — but it genuinely makes taking photos with my iPhone more practical and a lot more fun.

It started as a way to solve one specific video-shooting problem, but I found myself reaching for it far more often than I expected...

One of the great divides in the world of compact cameras has always been whether or not you need a viewfinder. The old guard of camera enthusiasts used to get very worked up about electronic viewfinders (EVF) versus optical ones, but EVFs are now so good that almost no one cares anymore.

But whether optical or electronic, a viewfinder offers one very practical advantage over composing on the rear screen, particularly when shooting in harsh sunlight. Even with the screen brightness cranked all the way up, it's still hard to make out the image when the sun is intense, and you also have to deal with screen reflections.

Although in London this has historically not been that big an issue, this summer has brought record-breaking heatwaves, and frankly, I think the last time I saw a cloud or some rain was roughly thirty years ago.

But for me, there's something more to it than that. I also feel there's a psychological difference between looking through a viewfinder, where you only see what's within the frame of the photo, versus looking at the screen, where everything around it is also visible. Sometimes it's precisely that feeling that makes me reach for a standalone camera rather than my iPhone.

When I was choosing a video camera a few years ago, the Blackmagic Pocket Cinema Camera 4K was the obvious hot pick, but the lack of a viewfinder gave me pause. In the end I decided it wasn't a big issue for me, as I'd mostly be using it indoors, and when I needed to use it outside, attaching a large screen with a sun hood solved most of the problems.

Still, there are times when I want to shoot in a more compact setup rather than lugging around the whole rig with a screen attached, so I found a simple accessory for use outdoors. It's a combination sun hood and magnifying lens that magnetically attaches to the camera's rear screen, giving an approximation of an optical viewfinder.

I had an upcoming shoot where I'd be filming with both the BMPCC 4K and my iPhone 16 Pro Max. I did a quick test on location and found the viewfinder accessory really helped. Since the BMPCC 4K and iPhone screens are pretty similar in size, I wondered if this accessory could be made to work on the iPhone.

Of course the iPhone doesn't have magnets, but the iPhone is light enough that holding it against the magnifying lens manually is no problem at all. To my surprise, it worked remarkably well, especially since I typically use the camera control button as my shutter.

Since then, I've found myself using this setup in many situations, enjoying both the benefit of seeing the screen more clearly in harsh sunlight and that sense of immersion. My iPhone became my main camera a long time ago, and with this DIY modification, I feel that even more often, just taking my phone with me is enough.

Genius or madness? Let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you're the latter, the product I bought appears to be discontinued, and I haven't yet seen anything similar designed specifically for screens larger than three inches. If you find one, please drop a link in the comments.
